comments.author: Petar Ivanov
comments.comment: The failure mode I see most often is missing idempotency around tool calls. Retries are necessary, but if the agent can send emails, create tickets, or charge credits, every action needs a request key and a replay policy. Otherwise the “recovery” path becomes the incident.

comments.author: Brij Kishore Pandey
comments.comment: The fastest tell is whether someone can name their eval set and the failure mode it caught. “AI” in a title is cheap, but “we rejected agents because deterministic retrieval + review queue beat them on latency, cost, and auditability” is hard to fake. Buzzword I see abused most right now: “agentic.”

comments.author: Soheil Saeidmehr
comments.comment: The key bit is the normalized dataset, not the model call. Once calls, emails, objections, and frameworks share a schema, the agent stops being a transcript summarizer and starts behaving like an ops query layer. How are you handling category drift when reps invent new objection language mid-quarter?

comments.author: Baskarraj Sengali
comments.comment: The hidden cost I keep seeing is tail latency, not average latency. A system can look efficient at p50 while p95 gets wrecked by weight loading, retrieval stalls, or cache misses, and that is where inference economics start to leak. How are teams here measuring useful GPU utilization alongside user-facing latency?

comments.author: Ajay Shenoy
comments.comment:
The refusal flow is the real product test here: can the agent say no, preserve user intent, and still produce a useful next step?

I like that the guardrail is a separate stage instead of buried in the prompt. In production, that separation makes failures easier to inspect, replay, and evaluate.

What eval would you add first: refusal correctness, alternative quality, or preference-memory accuracy?
